newsitem.title: USA: Strike poses little threat to UPS finances - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Strike poses little threat to UPS finances - analysts.

text.p: United Parcel Service is so big a powerhouse that it would be hard to imagine the Teamsters strike lasting long enough to do much harm to the company's financial health, Wall Street analysts said Tuesday.

Even as UPS threatened to lay off thousands of workers to compensate for losses, analysts pointed to a $500 million cash mountain and a $4.5 billion line of bank credit as signs that the leading parcel delivery company was still far from true financial hardship.
"They have huge resources to withstand any strike," Standard & Poor's analyst Philip Baggaley said.

"The company has said they're losing tens of millions of dollars a day. But when you have a $4.5 billion credit line and a very strong financial position, obviously you still can afford to stand some pain."

S&P, which assesses the credit risks of corporate and public sector debt, reaffirmed its highest, triple-A rating on UPS debt Tuesday. But S&P also said the outlook for the company had been dimmed by the onset of the strike.

Baggaley said questions about the strike's impact on UPS operations had mainly to do with the cost structure of any prospective new Teamster contract and the ability of the Atlanta-based company to retain customers hurt by the walkout.
Asked how long the strike would have to last before it posed a real threat to the company's financial standing, he said: "It would have to be so long that it's way beyond anything we would imagine."
Analysts dismissed a claim by UPS that its strike-related losses were so great that more than 15,000 Teamster jobs would be eliminated even if the walkout ended by Friday.

"I think it's partly sabre rattling. It's probably also some pressure tactic on their part to get the union to come back to the bagaining table," said Martine Nowicki, an analyst with Moody's Investors Service Inc.
"This strike has lasted a week. If a triple-A company cannot withstand a week or two of a strike, then obviously we don't have the right rating on it to begin with."

S&P said in its report that while the permanent loss of some customers was possible, the strike had shown UPS competitors incapable of picking up more than a fraction of the company's normal daily volumes.
Although UPS has built its public image on friendly and unpretentious service, behind the scenes its vast wealth places it among the biggest U.S. blue-chip corporations.

The company, whose privately issued stock is held mainly by its own executives, ranks 37th on the Fortune 500 list of leading U.S. companies by virtue of its $22.4 billion in annual revenues. That puts it ahead of such household names as Coca-Cola Co. and Intel Corp.

UPS also is more widely admired by senior business executives than even Microsoft Corp. Its rare triple-A debt rating puts the company among the elite of U.S. industrial corporations. Only nine other companies, including such notables as General Electric Co. and Exxon Corp., are rated triple-A.
"This is among the very, very blue-chip companies," Nowicki said.
Another advantage the company has in its struggle against the Teamsters is that much of the stock is held by a clutch of executives now engaged in marshaling UPS resources against the union.
UPS Chief Executive Officer Kelly, for example, owns 180,655 UPS shares. At a current in-house value of $30.50 a share, his stake would be worth $5.5 million.

"It doesn't change the basic issues they have to grapple with, with the union. But it gives them more flexibility to pursue them as the management team sees fit. They can focus on the longer-term strategy without worrying about where their share price is right at the moment," Baggaley said.
A miniscule amount of shares are held by rank-and-file employees, including those now staffing picket lines.
